HuleEdu: The Essay-Scoring System

Last updated September 1, 2026.
Browse the research code →Codeberg repository ↗

About This Document

The system behind my research has grown past the point where a description in passing works. This document explains what the system is made of, how a score is produced, how I test whether the scores mean anything, and which systems process student text when the instrument runs. It assumes no background in machine learning or programming. The results it mentions are current at the last-updated date shown above, and none of them is final.

What the System Is

HuleEdu is a research instrument for developing and evaluating methods that help teachers assess and grade essays written by learners of English in Sweden. It is intended to sort essays, suggest likely grades for straightforward cases, and identify essays that require closer human judgment. Teachers shape the instrument by comparing essays and selecting anchors that represent writing quality in a course or assessment context. These judgments provide the reference standard used to evaluate and calibrate the models. The instrument's assessments must be open to inspection so that teachers can understand and explain them.

The Essays the System Learns From

A scoring method must learn from essays that already have trusted human scores, and it needs many of them. The system works with two collections of essays.

The first collection is ELLIPSE↗, a public research corpus, or collection of texts assembled for study. It contains roughly 6,500 essays written by school-age learners of English in the United States, each scored independently by two trained human raters on a scale from 1 to 5 in half-point increments. Because the corpus was released in anonymized form for research use, it contains no identifiable students.

Because two trained raters scored every essay independently, the corpus also shows how often and how far trained raters disagree with each other. That record of human disagreement becomes the benchmark against which the system's agreement must be read, and I return to it in the section on evaluation.

The second collection is private Swedish research material rather than a public dataset. It contains 281 prompt-resolvable essays written by my own upper-secondary students in English 5, English 6, and English 7, together with the assessment exemplars associated with their national tests. These courses are now named English 1, English 2, and English 3, so both naming systems occur in the retained material. The essays use anonymous identifiers; only my separate private records connect them to individual students.

ELLIPSE provides thousands of essays, each rated twice by trained raters, so it is the material the methods learn from. The Swedish essays do not have comparable double-rated reference scores, and 281 essays are far too few to learn from. They therefore serve a different purpose by providing transfer evidence: evidence about whether a method learned from one population also applies to another. The system learns nothing from the Swedish essays.

How a Score Is Produced

The system estimates essay quality through three separate methods. The feature-based scorer and hybrid scorer each produce a score for one essay, while comparative judgment ranks essays from pairwise decisions. Figure 1 shows how the three methods produce separate outputs that can be compared or combined.

Figure 1. How a score is produced. The feature-based and hybrid scorers process one essay at a time, while comparative judgment processes essay pairs. Each method produces its own output. The outputs are compared or combined only after all three methods have finished. Comparative judgment is not trained on the human scores.

The Feature-Based Scorer

The feature-based scorer estimates essay quality from 30 named linguistic measures. These measures describe accuracy, sentence structure, vocabulary, task relevance, and organization. The complete feature inventory explains how each measure is calculated.

A regression model learns how the measures relate to the human scores in ELLIPSE and combines them into one estimate for each essay. Because the measures retain their individual meanings, their contributions to an estimate can be inspected.

The Hybrid Scorer

The hybrid scorer combines named linguistic measures with an embedding produced by DeBERTa-v3. The embedding represents the whole essay as 768 numbers. A regression model learns from the human-scored ELLIPSE essays how to combine this representation with 36 scalar measures and produce one estimate.

The hybrid scorer agrees more closely with the ELLIPSE human scores than the feature-based scorer does. However, the individual numbers in the embedding do not have named linguistic meanings. Comparing the two scorers therefore separates what can be achieved with defined linguistic measures from what is gained by adding a whole-essay representation.

Comparative Judgment

Comparative judgment estimates relative essay quality through pairwise decisions. A judge selects the stronger essay in each pair, after which a Bradley-Terry model uses the pattern of decisions to place the essays on a shared ranking.

In the current research system, the judge is a large language model. The method does not use the linguistic measures, essay embeddings, or ELLIPSE grades. Teacher panels can use the same procedure to establish the human reference against which the model judge is evaluated. Because comparative judgment produces a ranking, it can also represent differences between essays that receive the same grade.

How I Know Whether It Works

Models are evaluated on essays that were excluded from training. The primary evaluation also excludes complete writing tasks. This tests whether a scorer can assess essays written for an unfamiliar task instead of relying on topic-specific patterns. A separate portion of the official ELLIPSE test partition remains sealed until declared evaluation checkpoints.

Results are reported with quadratic weighted kappa and mean absolute error. Quadratic weighted kappa gives greater weight to larger differences between predicted and human scores. Mean absolute error reports the average difference in scale points. Together, they describe agreement across the scale and the typical size of an error.

The two trained ELLIPSE raters have a quadratic weighted kappa of about 0.58 across the double-rated essays. The scorers are evaluated against the raters' combined score, so this value is not a ceiling for model agreement. It establishes that the reference scores contain variation between human judgments.

Few ELLIPSE essays occur near the ends of the scoring scale. On the official test partition, the hybrid scorer overestimated essays scored 1 or 2 by an average of 0.240 points. It underestimated essays scored 4 or 5 by 0.244 points, and essays scored 4.5 or 5 by 0.390 points. Counterfactual tests improved separation between high-scoring and middle-scoring essays by changing the effective influence of existing inputs, although overall accuracy did not improve. The current scorer therefore uses some available information at the upper end inefficiently.

ELLIPSE provides an official training partition and test partition, which allows comparison with published systems evaluated on the same material. In August 2026, the frozen HuleEdu scorers were evaluated once on 2,567 of the 2,571 official test essays. The hybrid scorer achieved a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.756 with the broader training set described later in this document and 0.744 without it. Its mean absolute error was 0.30 scale points.

Choi et al. (2026) report a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.726 on the official partition. Their system differs from HuleEdu in its training data and model design. The comparison therefore benchmarks two complete systems on the same test partition rather than isolating one modeling choice. The HuleEdu results reported here come from the hybrid scorer without comparative judgment.

The three methods were also compared in an experiment on one ELLIPSE writing task. The equal average of their outputs produced the strongest held-out point estimate. Paired resampling supported its advantage over the feature-based scorer and comparative judgment, while the difference from the hybrid scorer remained unresolved. The hybrid scorer was stronger on the out-of-fold training essays.

Open Research

The sections below distinguish completed changes from the research questions that remain open.

Verified Corrections for Second-Language Errors

Ordinary spelling and grammar checkers miss some errors that are typical of second-language writing, and some proposed corrections change the writer's meaning. I therefore use one cumulative correction treatment: eligible LanguageTool repairs are combined with validated exact-span lexical repairs for errors that ordinary tools could not recover. Only safe, single-token lexical pairs enter the durable dictionary. Grammar or syntax changes, compounds, ambiguous contextual substitutions, and multi-token rewrites remain outside it. Once a pair has been accepted, applying it is a deterministic lookup that involves no model call.

An applied correction still counts as evidence of an error in the essay. The repaired text feeds only the measures that require grammatical analysis, while the fixed whole-essay representation continues to use the original unrepaired essay. This preserves both the error evidence and the writer's original text.

The cumulative correction method was evaluated on 5,470 training essays and tested once on 2,567 official-test essays. On the official test, the transparent scorer reached 0.649 agreement and an average error of 0.388 scale points, while the hybrid scorer reached 0.749 agreement and an average error of 0.317 scale points.

The evaluated correction method was then adopted in the current scorers. This adoption reused the already tested methods and did not produce a second set of evaluation results.

Broadening the Training Set

An earlier training generation used 3,479 essays. A later, broader training set recovered 1,563 additional eligible essays while keeping the official test partition separate. In the August benchmark, the hybrid scorer's agreement increased from 0.744 to 0.756. Subgroup results were mixed, so the broader training set helped overall but did not solve every weakness across the scale.

Comparative Judgment as a Source of Relative Quality

The scoring models learn from the scores assigned to individual essays. A score groups essays into broad bands, but it does not say which essay is better within a band. Comparative judgment supplies that relationship by recording which of two essays is better written.

An initial experiment trained a separate model directly from earlier comparative judgments. It predicted comparative decisions for essays that were not part of its training set better than the score-based baseline did. The existing score-based model still predicted human grades more accurately, and simple attempts to combine the two did not improve grade prediction. The comparative decisions therefore contain learnable information, but the project has not yet shown how to use it to improve the scorer.

The current work separates two questions. First, candidate model judges receive the same short instructions and the same fixed essay pairs, including both essay orders. This makes it possible to compare their agreement with the human score ordering, their consistency, their token use, and their cost without tailoring the test to one model. Second, later experiments will test whether the resulting pairwise evidence improves the scorer beyond the absolute scores. The comparisons cover several writing tasks and include both within-task and between-task pairs. If the learned ordering reflects a shared aspect of writing quality, it should transfer across tasks; this remains unproven.

Linking the ELLIPSE Scale to the Swedish Course Continuum

ELLIPSE scores are defined for one population of learners in the United States. Whether they order Swedish upper-secondary essays sensibly is an open question, and it is the question the 281 scored Swedish essays exist to probe. The retained experiment places the anonymous classroom essays described earlier on ELLIPSE's 1-to-5 scale. The ELLIPSE midpoint is 3. English 5 cohort medians are roughly 3.2 to 3.5, English 6 medians are 3.9 to 4.1, and the usable English 7 cohort median is about 4.3. The difference is largest between English 5 and English 6 and smaller between English 6 and English 7. These are classroom cohorts, not the separate official anchor essays. This public comparison uses English 7 VT2017 because the later sample is too small.

The English 7 distance is substantial on this scale. Only about one in twenty ELLIPSE predictions are 4 or higher, compared with about two in three to three in four predictions for English 7 VT2017. This is why a difference of about 1.3 scale points matters: the English 7 cohort is concentrated in a region that is only the thin upper tail of the ELLIPSE predictions.

Figure 3. Comparison of Swedish course cohorts with ELLIPSE. The ELLIPSE curve is schematic. The course positions summarize the same classroom-cohort comparison described above. The English 7 position uses VT2017 and does not use the separate official anchor essays or the very small VT2018 sample.

The two populations differ in a way that may explain the ordered course differences. ELLIPSE is a corpus of designated English learners, and students who become proficient leave that population. The corpus therefore has a proficiency cap. Swedish school English has no such cutoff, because every student takes the courses regardless of proficiency. If this reading is correct, ELLIPSE may overlap most with Swedish Year 9 and the start of English 5, while the higher courses produce increasingly higher score distributions. That possibility connects directly to the supervisory group's work on using automated essay scoring and language technology to support Year 9 assessment. I do not yet have ninth-grade national-test essays, so this is a research hypothesis to test, not a finding. I do not claim that ELLIPSE and Swedish school English share one construct. The work measures the overlap and differences between the scales and identifies the score regions in which the models remain reliable enough to support assessment. A later study will add official assessment exemplars as candidates for anchor work, allowing the comparison to be related to Swedish grading standards in a way my own course cohorts cannot. Their number and selection remain part of the study design, and an official grade does not make an exemplar ground truth. Its role in the anchor set depends on the teacher panel's interpretation and mediation.

The Teacher Panel

The comparisons so far measure models against rater scores. The reference that matters for the project is teacher judgment. The planned teacher panel develops an anchor set: selected essays together with the teachers' judgments, rationales, disagreements, compromises, and shared interpretation of the grading standard. The anchor essays therefore do more than mark points on a scale. They retain the professional reasoning through which the panel defines and discusses writing quality. The resulting anchor set is then compared with the comparative-judgment ranking and the ELLIPSE-trained scorers. In this design the instrument is the thing being checked, and teacher judgment is the thing it is checked against. That ordering is a standing commitment of the project. However well the lanes agree with each other or with the ELLIPSE raters, the question that decides whether the instrument can support Swedish assessment work is whether its outputs hold up against the judgment of the teachers who do that work.

Where Computation Happens and Where Data Goes

Student text can be processed through a consumer chat interface, a provider's API, or a self-hosted model. These are different technical and contractual arrangements, so the interface alone does not determine how the text is handled.

In a chat interface, a person submits text through the provider's consumer product, which then handles it under that product's terms and the account's data controls. For personal ChatGPT workspaces, for example, OpenAI allows users to turn off the use of new conversations for model training and documents the setting here.

An API is not a separate data destination. It is a technical interface through which one program sends a defined request to another service and receives the result. The research pipeline uses APIs for external model calls, so its code determines what enters each request, while the provider's API terms determine how that request is handled. For the OpenAI API used here, inputs and outputs are not used to train OpenAI's models by default. Consumer chat controls therefore do not govern these API requests.

A self-hosted model instead runs on hardware that I control, which means that no external model provider receives the text during that processing. Most processing in this project is self-hosted on Hemma, the server I built at home. It runs the embedding model, parser, error-checking programs, and local language models, while the two regression scorers are small enough to run locally on ordinary hardware, including a phone.

The retained research records document two categories of text sent to external providers. One is essay text from the public, anonymized ELLIPSE corpus. An earlier comparative-judgment experiment sent ELLIPSE essay pairs to a provider-hosted OpenAI model in mid-2026. The current judge evaluation compares a provider-hosted open-weight model with a local version using the same anonymous ELLIPSE comparisons. The hosted evaluation sends the essay text to the provider, while the local evaluation keeps it on Hemma. The correction experiments have also sent ELLIPSE text to provider-hosted models, but they have not used Swedish student essays.

The other is de-identified Swedish essay text. Earlier model-judge work compared Swedish student essays with anchor essays used as fixed reference points. Several raters had assessed and discussed each anchor essay, so its agreed score represented a shared interpretation of the test rather than one person's judgment. That completed work sent the Swedish essays and anchor essays to the same provider-hosted OpenAI model used in the earlier ELLIPSE experiment. It is separate from the planned human teacher panel: model-judge results cannot create the teacher-mediated anchor set or determine its reference values. Each request contained the judging instructions, the writing task, and essay text under anonymous identifiers. The identifier-to-student record was kept separately and was not part of the request.

Figure 2 shows that retained data-processing contract.

Figure 2. Processing locations and external transmissions. Hemma, my home server, performs all local essay processing. External comparative-judgment and correction requests contain only the declared essay text under anonymous identifiers. Comparative-judgment requests contain ELLIPSE pairs or de-identified Swedish essays and anchor essays. Correction requests contain ELLIPSE text only. The identifier-to-student record remains offline on my home server and is never transmitted, so no request can connect an essay to a student.

I want to reduce external use further. An open-weight model publishes the learned numerical weights required to run it on hardware under my control, although its training data and training procedure may remain closed. Small trials identified Gemma 4 31B as the strongest local candidate tested so far. The next evaluation will apply the same fixed essay comparisons to a provider-hosted version and a version running on Hemma. It will compare their agreement with the human score ordering, consistency, processing time, token use, and provider cost. The full result is not yet available, so the local model is not yet the accepted comparative judge.

What Can Be Claimed Today

The system can produce essay-quality estimates from three partly distinct methods. In the held-out experiment, their equal average had the strongest point estimate, although paired resampling did not clearly distinguish it from the combined scorer and the combined scorer was stronger on the out-of-fold training essays. On the official ELLIPSE test partition, the hybrid scorer has also agreed with the human raters more closely than a published comparison system (Choi et al., 2026), under the descriptive comparison stated in the section on evaluation. The system's estimates are most reliable in the middle of the 1 to 5 scale, and the weakening at the extremes has been measured and quantified. Its evidence about Swedish student writing is transfer evidence from an American learner corpus, ordered plausibly by course level but not yet anchored to Swedish grading standards. The instrument can therefore support research on assessment, and it cannot yet support assessment decisions, which is the boundary the teacher panel and the exemplar work are designed to test.
